6*pi*a*(eta)*v = >mg

and the dust will no longer float.

posts.content_md:
So, you're telling me that you have swirling dust in the air. You zap the dust, reflection? transmission? Let's assume that somehow the dust particles are suspended and stable. This negates the necessity of a pulse laser. Whether or not a real pulse can do a real hologram of swirling dust is now a secondary condition.

Let's say reflection. Then you're presumably talking about a single beam Denisyuk? So the beam goes through the plate, hitsdust particles in the air, and then reflects enough object beam back onto the plate to create a hologram of these very small dust particles. You now look through the plate and see dust particles.IS this a reasonable description? OK, so the obvious question is: will the dust particles reflect enough of the beam to create a strong enough object beam.It seems to me that this depends on the number and density of the particles. It seems to follow that one dust particle would certainly reflect whatever the (how can I say"capture cross section of a dust particle"?) Oh Ok, the area of the beam covered by the dust particle. Now a dust particle is about 10 microns or less in diameter. I hope you give me this since we are talking specifically about dust. This is about 20 lambda or less . So you have a structure of width 20 lambda or less interrupting a beam. I expect this will diffract. So now the return object beam has a superimposed diffraction pattern around it. Since speckle is also a diffractive/interference effect, the diffractive pattern from the dust will compete with the speckle. Which will be larger? The average size of speckle is also on the order of a few microns, so this question hinges on the distance from the plate to the dust particle. Certainly I see this as a limiting factor. The dust will be an effective point particle with a dimension small enough to be an effective aperture. Since I'm assuming that we're talking a real dust particle, how much light will the dust particle radiate back? It's certainly possible to calculate the diffraction pattern and the reflectivity of a perfect sphere, but dust is not a perfect sphere. So we have an inhomogenous surface. If the structure itself is on the order of 10 or so microns, I think we can safely assume that the surface features will be of the order of about a micron, or roughly 2 lambda. So now we have surface features of 2 lambda each acting as a source of new waves a la Fresnel. These new waves will also mutually interfere and diffract. What will now be the net outgoing wavefront? And, what will be it's intensity? Considering these extremely small features, I think I can argue that there will be significant absorption and loss due to mutual diffractive effects from these surface features. So, I doubt you'll get more than a few percent of light back. Thus, taking the inverse square law into consideration, even in a perfect world, you have a ratio of probably close to 100:1. I would argue that the fringe modulation at 100:1 would be negligible. Of course, you could say that the dust particle is extremely close to the plateand so increase this modulation, but noweher near the values you'd expect to get a hologram from. These are general statements evaluating the possibility of taking a hologram of a staionary dust particle. If the dust particle were now moving, the modulation would further decrease because it's velocity would cause it to move more than one of it's diameters/sec. Thus there's a constant drop in object beam intensity depending on the rate at which the particle is receeding in the z direction. Since exposure is dependant on the respective intensities of object and reference and since reference is constant while object is decreasing, there is now a race condition. Now add a few more dust particles. Each of these will again be point scatterers positioned randomly in space. I can do the calculation (but I know you'll scream if I do ) but it seems evident that there will be a rapidly fluctuating set of low frequency gratings. Since these gratings are rapidly fluctuating, the average illumination on the plate will be uniform. I haven't even considered what will happen if the dust particles are revolving around an axis within it's structure, but the phase changes involved in this kind of motion at the plate is very interesting. I won't go into details because it involves a theorem! There are a number of other problems as well but these are the major ones I can see. Other possible problems will occur if the dust is charged (as it might well be through friction and passage through the air) and so there's a mutual repellant action oif dust particles. You now have to calculate the phase changes caused by this "dust dance"as well as more complicated motions such as rotation of two (or more) particles around a common axis between the particles. There's also the electrostaic attraction of the dust to the plate itself. As the plate is so much larger than the particle, the particle will have a high acceleration. This acceleration will depend on whether or not the particles trajectory takes it to the center of the plate or the edge. There's also the effect of a particle going around the edge of the plate to the backside. This will cause a point scatterer behind the plate interfering with one in front. 

Note: no theorems, no mathematics, a few technical terms ("phase", "diffraction", "interference" etc) which I hope you don't scream too loudly at, since it's impossible to discuss holography without them.

[quote="Dinesh"] No scientific argument really ends with a ta-daa (except cold fusion-type arguments!)

[quote]

Indeed - wrong arguments just slowly fade away, and cold fusion is not quite dead yet. Maybe a better example would be the Michaelson/Morley disproof of the ether hypothesis? Even that probably took many years to become fully accepted.

Consider the following thought experiment:

A porcelain cat is moving in some random direction at speeds up to 1 m/sec. An attempt is made to make a hologram of it using a 1 ns pulsed laser of sufficient power to properly expose the plate. (much shorter pulse widths are of course available) The cat moves at most 1 nm during the exposure, much less than a wavelength of visible light, the fringes are not smeared, and we have a nice hologram. 

The porcelain cat is shrunk down to dust particle size, say 1-100 microns, and replicated, so we have thousands of little cats moving in random directions. Are they still visible? Yes - if the contrast against the background is good, we can easily detect them, as we can see dust in a sunbeam. Can we make a hologram showing their instantaneous position? Yes, one could consider the big cat as a whole bunch of micro-cat point sources flying in close formation and if we could make a hologram of that, why should a micro-cat be any different? 

nice reference on dust with size chart here:

[http://www.oznet.ksu.edu/library/hlsaf2/ncr393.pdf](http://www.oznet.ksu.edu/library/hlsaf2/ncr393.pdf)

posts.content_md:
[quote:d83c8f710c="TomB"]Maybe a better example would be the Michaelson/Morley disproof of the ether hypothesis? Even that probably took many years to become fully accepted. [/quote:d83c8f710c]

Actually it didn't. Michelson/Morley did not "disprove" the hypothesis. They set out to measure the earth's velocity wrt the ether, which they took for granted. To them ether was no hypothesis. The null result was the surprise and Lorentz's hypothesis of electron elongation was the "best" explanation. However, the elongation of the electron was an ad hoc explanation which Lorentz never fully justified. Einstein made the ether irrelevant (not non-existant as the popular media have you believe) by removing it as an absolute inertial frame. When he also postulated the constancy of the velocity of light in all inertial frames and, from this, derived a set of transformation equations, these equations turned out to be the very ones Lorentz had derived under the assumption of electron elongation. Einstein's was attempting to resolve the inconsistency between the fact that mechanical phenomena were invariant under a Galilean transformation, but electromagnetic phenomena, the Maxwell equations, were not. He felt that all natural phenomena in all inertial frames should be invariant under the same transformations. The "dismissal" of the ether was a consequence of the postulates under which the relativistic transformations were derived and was instantly recognised as such. They were not a consequence of the tranformation equations themselves. Of course, you can argue the postulates were ad hoc but, so far, relativity has stood all experimental tests. I have a fascinating book of the early work, including the Lorentz paper on electron elongation and another evaluating "field theories" going back to Descartes "plenum" field theory, which I will be glad to send you, if you're interested in ether and field theories.

Anyway, back to micro-cats 

First of all, what are the sizes of our dust particles? You say a maximum of 100nm, the paper you quoted says 1-50nm and I approixmated at 10nm. There's two orders of magnitude there between our figures. One reason I never put firgures in, just derive the equations! Anyway, the macrocat will not diffract (visible) light, the microcat will, depending on it's size. The structure of any reflected light is the far field Fraunhofer diffraction pattern. The larger an object is, the less the diffractive structure is visible, and conversely, the smaller an object is the more prominent is it's far field Franhofer pattern. Without actually calculating it, I'd suggest that a 10nm particle will have a significant diffractive patern. If the particle is uniformly round, this will be an diverging Airy disc. (Hence the pinhole, by the way). Thus each dust particle will form a set of low frequency gratings superimposed on the interference pattern. This will be very small for a macrocat, but as I say possibly significant on dust motes. If the dust particle is 100nm across, we may be getting to a point whereh the low frequency diffractive pattern is small as a ratio of the reflected light. Again, this ratio needs to be calculated. to find this critical size. In your paper I believe, without reading the references in the paper , they were using electrnic techniues to isolate the diffrative pattern and calculate the velocity from this. I can't remember, but I think I mentioned Doppler shifting in my original argument. I had doubts whether the doppler shift would be enough to detect, but since these authors seem to be relying on the variation of the far field pattern due to Doppler shifts, I guess it can matter. If I did mention Doppler, I was a little nervous since Kaveh would not have liked a reference to a technical term such as "Doppler shift".

The dust particle may be visible against a light of a sunbeam background only because our eyes are very good at discerning edge effects. I'd suggest that if the dusty sunbeam were to directly impinge on your eyes you would not be ably to see the dust motes. The holographic plate will be directly illuminated with the reference beam which will be hundreds of times more intense than the reflected light from a dust particle. Visibility alone does not indicate the possibility of good ratio. The eye is a logarithmic detector with sophisticated mechanisms for detectting edges, tilts, colour variations etc. The holographic plate can only depend on direct, linear intensity variations. If the dust particles were somehow reflecting with a Lambertian profile, the reflectivity may improve, but so would the corresponding diffractive pattern.

Neither I nor the paper you quoted have analysed rotation. This would add a further Doppler shift across the diameter. I believe I mentioned it as a passing effect. Electrostatic forces, a particular problem with real dust, is also not analysed. 

A lot would also depend on the density of dust particles and their size.

Re the "if you can see it, you can make a hologram of it" argument, it seems from the cited dust reference that the motes seen in sunbeams are at the larger end of the scale, mostly lint at 50-100 microns, so this is how big I would make my micro-cats. 

Re holography of nanometer scale objects, I can see that it would be difficult to see a single particle without a microscope, but a dense cloud of such objects should be visible and therefore holographable - consider for example a patch of white paint, the pigment composed of titanium dioxide particles with size range 50-500 nm. We have all made holograms of white painted objects, so it is possible to make holograms of stationary swarms of nanoparticles, and from the previous argument, a pulsed laser of quite modest pulse narrowness should allow holography of moving clouds of such particles.

I was attempting to answer Dinesh's objections to the possibility of making a hologram of a swirling cloud of small particles (dust).

There seemed to be two main objections - the problem of motion, which is solved by using a pulsed laser, and the separate problem of visibility (would very tiny particles be too small to register interference patterns?). [quote:80b9ff7d58="Tom B."]I was attempting to answer Dinesh's objections to the possibility of making a hologram of a swirling cloud of small particles (dust).

There seemed to be two main objections - the problem of motion, which is solved by using a pulsed laser, and the separate problem of visibility. This is solved by appealing to "if it can be seen, it can be holographed", with paint used as an example of a densely packed swarm of (stationary) nanoparticles.[/quote:80b9ff7d58]

But again, aren't we exaggerating a metaphor. The original question was: Can a hologram be made of swirling dust. By this I thought was meant a particularly dusty room, as for instance opening a window onto a building site where a lot of dust gets swirled. I was modelling a swirling, randomly moving "cloud" of common household dust. Arguments have been given concerning organised particle motion, or particles of a given size in an organised layout. I have already said that these are possible. I have already mentioned that aerosol particles were measured using a holographic technique - holographic interferometry - in which, yes I believe a ruby pulse was used. There have been papers on velocity measurements of particles, as Tom has shown us.

However, a densely packed set of particles as in paint is not "swirling dust", so this takes the system out of the assumptions of the model. Also, a white painted surface consists of fairly large particulate structures, as compared to household dust, closely packed together. This close packing means that there is "optical correlation" between adjacent particles. There is no such correlation between dust motes in swirling dust.

[quote:80b9ff7d58="TomB"](would very tiny particles be too small to register interference patterns?)[/quote:80b9ff7d58]

As I've said, the "optical pattern" of anything at a distance is the far field FFraunhofer diffraction pattern. I won't derive this or go into the physics of far field diffraction, but it's explained in many textbooks. I recommend "Introduction to Fourier Optics" by Goodman ( [http://www.roberts-publishers.com/goodm ... raise.html](http://www.roberts-publishers.com/goodman/Goodpraise.html) ). In the case of "dust" as in my description of dust motes in a swirling cloud in the model I used, the structure of the far field fraunhofer pattern would overwhelm any uniform illumination. The individual phase componnets of the Fraunhofer pattern would interfere with the reference beam, however the beam modulation would be so low (again I stress dust motes in swirling household dust) that the fringe visibilty may not record, depending on the medium and it's properties.

This close packing means that there is "optical correlation" between adjacent particles. There is no such correlation between dust motes in swirling dust. Perhaps a dilute suspension of TIO2 pigment particles in water would be good test? It occurs to me that even without a pulsed laser (just using a regular CW laser) this might be an interesting experiment - a shallow glass dish filled with a cm or 2 of milky liquid over a test pattern that would be blurred/obscured by the milk. A horizontal reflection setup would be easiest. I would expect that most likely the particles would NOT be recorded, in which case the formerly invisible test pattern should become visible in the hologram, or (less likely) some of the particles would be recorded and appear as a diffuse glow. Either result would be interesting.

[quote=Tom B."]I would expect that most likely the particles would NOT be recorded, in which case the formerly invisible test pattern should become visible in the hologram[/quote]

Tom, a few days ago I did just this. I didn't expect to get too much as I was trying the experiement with a split beam, 15 second exposure. What I did was take a glass, it was a Remy Martin glass and has the Remy Martin writen down it's side from the lip to the base and set it up in the reference beam upside down. I then took another raw beam and allowed it to pass through the glass from left to right. When I was ready to make the hologram I took a cigarette and filled the glass with smoke and turned it upside down back in its original position. I studied this for a while. At first the smoke caused such diffusion that you could not see the writing at all at the back but after about 5 good minutes the smoke was not as dense and is seemed like a short stick of laser light was magically floating in the glass. This effect alone was pretty cool. But anyway, I refilled the glass and made two holograms. One after about a minute and one after about 5 minutes. Both holograms turned out, as can be seen by the light given off where the beam entered and exited the glass but the writing on the back of the glass was clearly visible. I even tried to look between the two light spots (where the laser light entered and exited) very closely to see if where the beam was, the writing was dimmer or different in any way. Even when I tilted the hologram to move the apparent space where the beam went through the back writing was still as visible as the rest of the writing. Even the first hologram, which I am sure the beam was so loudly diffused I could not see the writing and the beam was not crisp, in the hologram the writing could be see. Now the writing was dim I asssume as it was lit through the smoke from the original reference beam and I am sure the second (object) beam did not move as it recorded the light spots on the glass at the entry and exit of the glass. 

It was a fun experiement and was made with old plates. I will try again with fresh plates to see if I can get one that is bright. Again this was with a CW laser and a 15 second exposure.

Sure, of course. This would work. You're basically using a shadowgram technique. The milk, in your case, and the smoke in John's case, are just diffusion screens. In 1990 or so, I tried this technique with a model car, about 3" long, using a double exposure. One shot with the car and one with the car enveloped in smoke. The decals on the car were visible in both shots, ie were equally visible with and without smoke.

In fact, it just occurs to me that this may be a good test of a colour holographic/colour polarisation system. The TiO2 would Rayleigh scatter sideways. You'd get colour and polarisation data from the background test pattern. The idea just occured to me so I have to play with awhile.
